caseno: Writ Petition No. 10101 of 2012 with Writ Petition Nos. 2310 & 9936 of 2019.
lawyer:
AKM Fakhrul Islam with Md Humayun Kabir, Advocates—For the Petitioner. (Writ Petition No. 10101 of 2012)

None Appears--For the Petitioner. (Writ Petition No. 2310 of 2019 and Writ Petition No. 9936 of 2019)

M. Saquibuzzaman, Advocate—For the Respondent Nos. 2 and 3. (All the above Writ Petitions)

full_judgment:
Md Zakir Hossain, J: Since the questions of law involved in Writ Petition Nos. 10101 of 2012, 2310 of 2019 and 9936 of 2019 are almost same and identical, therefore, they are taken up together for hearing and be disposed of by this single judgment. 2. At the instance of the Small Traders Co-operative Bank Limited, represented by its the then Secretary, Abdul Kader Sarder, Writ Petition No. 10101 of 2012 was filed and upon hearing on 29-7-2012, the Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the respondent No. 2 shall not be directed to issue a certificate of approval under section 13 of the Co-operative Societies Ain, 2001 (the Ain, 2001) showing approval of the amended bye-law of the petitioner-Co-operative Bank passed in its Extra-ordinary General Meeting held on 29-4-2012 (Annexure-F) as submitted to the respondent No. 2, the Registrar, Department of Co-operatives (the Registrar) on 30-4-2012 under Rule 9(2) of the Co-operative Societies Rules, 2004 (the Bidhimala, 2004) for approval in the prescribed Form 4 (Annexure-G) and/or such other of further order or orders be passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. The Court was further pleased to direct the parties to maintain status quo in respect of functioning of the petitioner-Society through its branch offices across the country for a period of 6(six) months. Subsequently, the order of status quo has been extended from time to time. 3. Writ Petition No. 2310 of 2019 was filed by the Small Traders Co-operative Bank Limited, represented by its Secretary, Md Abul Hassan wherein this Court on 7-4-2019 issued Rule Nisi calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the operation of the Small Traders Co-operative Bank Limited in Netrakona and Mymensingh or in any other Districts in Bangladesh by the Managing Committee formed on 10-12-2015 as contained in Annexure-M should not be declared to have been done without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 4. Writ Petition No. 9936 of 2019 was filed by the Small Traders Co-operative Bank Limited, represented by its Chairman, Mirza Atiqur Rahman wherein this Court on 16-9-2019 issued Rule Nisi calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Samabay Samity (Shongshodhon) Ain, 2013 (the Ain, 2013) amending some provisions of the Ain, 2001 by repealing, substituting and incorporating provisions of sections 9, 9(3), 13, 13(1Ka), 13(1Kha), 23Ka, 23Kha, 23Ka(2)(3), 26(1), 26Kha and 29 therein, being violative of Articles 26, 29, 31, 38 and 40 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (the Constitution) as such ultra vires the Constitution as well as contrary to scheme of the Ain, 2001 should not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 5. For the purpose of disposal of the aforesaid Rules, the relevant facts, in brief, are as follows: In fact, the petitioner of the three writ petitions is Small Traders Bank Limited, which is a registered Co-operative Societies having been incorporated under the Bengal Co-operative Societies Act, 1940 on 17-7-1976 vide registration No. 1801, thereafter, on 28-6-2006 it was again registered under the Ain, 2001 and its bye-law. At the time of registration, the area of activities was in Narayanganj. On 14-4-2012, the Board of Directors of the petitioner-Society decided to amend its bye-law in order to change address of its registered office and extending its activities throughout the country. The proposed amendment was approved by the members of the petitioner-Society in its Extra-ordinary General Meeting dated 19-4-2012. Thereafter, the petitioner-Society on 30-4-2012 filed an application for approval of the proposed bye-law to the Registrar. Having received the said application, the Registrar did not pay any heed to this and by efflux of 60 days of receiving the said application, the proposed bye-law was deemed to have been approved by operation of law. Thereafter, on 18-7-2012 in its Extra-ordinary General Meeting, members of the petitioner-Society decided to change its registered office from Narayanganj to Dhaka and also decided to open branch offices as many as 75 different places of the country for carrying on its activities. Indeed in Writ Petition No. 10101 of 2012, the petitioner sought direction upon the Registrar for issuance of certificate of approval or registration so far it relates to proposed bye-law. 6. In the writ petition No. 2310 of 2019, the petitioner challenged the legality of the operation of the petitioner's activities in Netrakona and Mymenshingh or in any other districts in Bangladesh by the Managing Committee formed on 10-12-2015. In writ petition No. 9936 of 2019, the petitioner-Society challenged that the provisions of sections 9, 9(3), 13, 13(1Ka), 13(1Kha), 23Ka, 23(2)(3), 26(1), 26Kha and 29 of the Ain, 2013 are ultra vires to Articles 26, .29, 31, 38 of the Constitution and the scheme of the Ain, 2013. 7. Mr AKM Fakhrul Islam along with Mr Md Humayun Kabir, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner-Society took us through the Writ Petition No. 10101 of 2012, annexure thereto, relevant provisions of the Ain, 2001, along with the different provisions of the Ain, 2013 and bye-law of the petitioner-Society. Taking thread from Writ Petition No. 10101 of 2012, he submits that the Board of Directors of the petitioner-Society on 14-4-2012 decided to amend clause 3(Ka), 4(Ka) and 4(Kha) of its bye-law for changing address of its registered office from Narayanganj to Dhaka and extending its activities throughout the country and later on, by its Extra-ordinary General Meeting dated 29-4-2012 the proposed amendment of bye-law was accepted and accordingly, submitted to the Registrar for its approval on 30-4-2012 in accordance with the procedure prescribed in the Bidhimala, 2004. He further submits that after expiry of 60 days of receiving the proposed amendment of bye-law by the Rgistrar, deemed to have been approved by operation of law as embodied under section 13(1) of the Ain, 2001. He next submits that considering the deeming approval of bye-law, the petitioner-Society in its Extra-ordinary General Meeting dated 29-4-2012 decided to carry on activities throughout the country and as many as 75 different places, new branches of the petitioner-Society were launched and started functioning of the petitioner's society with full swing and after that, the Chairman of the petitioner-Society wrote a letter on 19-7-2012 to the Registrar for approval of its 75 branches throughout Bangladesh but the Registrar did not pay heed to this. 8. He next submits that this Court is legally competent to direct the Registrar to issue a certificate under section 13 of the Ain, 2001 showing approval of the amendment of the bye-law of the petitioner-Society. He further submits that by opening branch offices in different districts, the petitioner-Society has been carrying on its activities in accordance with law. He next submits that surprisingly, Bangladesh Bank, Rajshahi Branch by its letter dated 27-11-2019 addressing to the Deputy commissioner of Rajshahi, Chapainawabganj, Natore, Pabna, Kushtia, Chuadanga, and Meherpur stated very derogatory comments to the petitioner-Society which is colorable exercise of power and thereby, the petitioner's branch offices are under threat of closure although the branch offices were set up in accordance with the bye-law of the petitioner-Society. He further contends that if the petitioner-Society is not allowed to use the word Bank, that will tantamount to unequal treatment and, as such, that will be repugnant to Article 27 of the Constitution. He next submits that the Samabay Samity like the Sondip Central Co-operative Bank Ltd. and Dhaka Mercantile Co-operative Bank Ltd. are functioning by using the word Bank after the word Co-operative. He further submits that the petitioner-Society having fulfilled the requisite conditions of the Ain, 2001, the Bidhimala, 2004 and its bye-law decided to amend the same and thereafter, the proposed amendment was approved and submitted to the Registrar with a legitimate expectation to have a certificate of approval or registration. But unfortunately, due to the inaction of the Registrar, the petitioner-Society did not obtain any certificate and therefore, a direction should be made upon the Registrar for issuance of a certificate of approval, otherwise, it will entail serious prejudice to the petitioner-Society. He further submits that the very inaction of the Registrar in giving the certificate of approval of bye-law and the activities of inaction of the Registrar are violative of Articles 27, 31 and 38 of the Constitution. 9. At the fag end, he strongly submits that the proposed bye-law of the petitioner-Society deemed to have been approved in view of proviso and deeming clause appended to section 13(1) of the Ain, 2001, therefore, it does not require to take any step in view of the latest amendment the Ain, 2013. 10. None appears in Writ Petition Nos. 2310 of 2019 and 9936 of 2019 to press the Rules issued therein. Be that as it may, they will be disposed of on merit in order to prevent multiplicity of proceedings. 11. As against to this, Mr M. Saquib-uz-zaman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the Registrar, Department of Co-operatives submits that the petitioner-Society is doing unlawful and illegal acts by using the word Bank which is repugnant to the provisions of section 23A of the Ain, 2013. He next submits that the petitioner's conduct amply proves that it has not come with clean hands to seek equitable remedy, therefore, the writ petitions are not maintainable, hence, they are liable to be turned down to secure the ends of justice. 12. He further submits that the people of the country at large are being deceived by opening and operating branches of the petitioner's Society throughout the country without any approval of the Registrar and thereby, continuously negating and flouting the rule 12(2) of the Bidhimala, 2004. 13. He further submits that the decision of the petitioner in opening branches throughout the country is absolutely illegal in view of section 23A(1) of the Ain, 2013. 14. He also submits that the Ain, 2013 incorporated the various provisions to meet the challenge of the Co-operatives are presumed to be constitutionally valid law and the legislature by applying its wisdom enacted the AM, 2013, keeping conformity to the Constitution and the Ain, 2001. He further submits that mere assertion that the Ain, 2013 is unconstitutional is not enough but heavy burden lies upon the petitioner to prove that some of provisions of the Ain, 2013 were repugnant to the Constitution and the scheme of the Ain, 2001. 15. He further submits that mere inaction on the part of the Registrar does not ipso facto entitle the petitioner to obtain the certificate of approval as argued by the learned lawyer of the petitioner. Finally, he submits that the earlier provisions of section 13 have been amended by substitution of new provision; therefore, the earlier provision has lost its validity. Finally, he submits that the petitioner in order to perpetuate its illegal activities i.e. doing co-operative businees throughout the country filed series of writ petitions, and hence, the Rules are liable to be discharged. 16. Now, the pertinent issues are— i. Whether the provisions of sections 9, 9(3), 13, 13(1Ka), 13(1Kha), 23Ka, 23Kha, 23Ka(2)(3), 26(1), 26Kha, 29 of the Ain, 2013 are ultra vices to Articles 26, 29, 31, 38 and 40 of the Constitution as well as contrary to scheme of the Ain, 2001; ii. Whether the petitioner-Society is legally empowered to use the word Bank after Co-operative Society despite the Ain of 2013; iii. Whether the petitioner-Society is legally entitled to obtain certificate of registration under section 13 of the Ain, 2001 showing approval of the proposed amendment of bye-law of the petitioner. 17. We have perused all the writ petitions, affidavit-in-oppositions and annexures filed thereto along with the submissions advanced by the learned Advocates of the parties and the legal positions intricately involved in this case with extreme care and attention and serious-ness as they deserve. Bank falls under one category of financial institutions known as banking financial institutions. A bank is known as financial intermediaries that act as middlemen between depositors or suppliers of funds and lenders who are the users of funds. The main tasks of a banking financial institution are to accept deposits and then to use those funds to offer loans to its customers, who will in turn utilize them to fund purchases, education, to expand business, to invest in development, etc. A bank also acts as a payment agent by offering a host of payment services including debit cards, credit cards, cheque facility, direct deposit facilities, bank drafts, etc. A bank’s ability to lend out funds is determined by the amount of excess reserves and the ratio of cash reserves held by the bank. It is relatively easy for a bank to raise funds as certain accounts such as demand deposits, pay no interest to the account holder. A bank makes money investing the money that they receive from deposits, sometimes in assets and financial securities, but mostly in loans. 43. The main difference between banking financial institutions and non-banking financial institutions is that a banking financial institution can accept deposit into various savings and demand deposit accounts, which cannot be done by a non-banking financial institution. A non-banking financial institution provides a variety of services including some that overlap with banking financial institutions such as grant loans, offer financial advice, investment in financial securities, leasing of equipment, etc. In addition, non-banking financial institutions also offer additional services such as insurance coverage, under-writing activities, market making, etc. The primary purposes in depositing funds in banks are convenience, interest income, and safety, whereas the primary purpose in investing funds in non-banking financial institutions is to gain additional income. 44. "Deeming Provisions in the Indian Insolvency Law" authored by Surbhi Kapur has spelt out the consequence of deeming provision in the Statute. She states to the effect— Deeming provisions are a common attribute of legislative enactments worldwide. The term 'deem' is derived from the old English word 'domas' which meant 'judgment or law'. The Concise Oxford Dictionary, (8th ed.), defines the verb 'to deem' as 'believe, 'consider, judge, or count, to be.' Webster's Ninth New Collegiate Dictionary provides the following meanings: 'to come to think or judge: consider; to have an opinion: believe.' Black's Law Dictionary (9th ed.), gives as the main definition of the verb 'deem' to treat (something) as if (1) it were really something else, or (2) it had qualities that it does not have.' Bennion Statutory Interpretation (3rd ed. 1997, p. 735), states: 'Deeming provisions Acts often deem things to be what they are not. In construing a deeming provision, it is necessary to bear in mind the legislative purposes.' (Web page supra) 59. Surbhi Kapur drew the conclusion of the aforementioned article with the following observation: Deeming provisions while frequently resorted to by the Courts must be utilised prudently. Since such provisions are not operative components of a legislative enactment their interpretive import is limited. Therefore, while enacting such provisions the legislature needs to assess the consequences of such an automatic conferment of status. Some determination would be required to be conducted before the conferment of such a status on the concerned persons. It may, unknowingly, lead to excessive delegated legislation, thereby twisting the real legislative intent. Despite these concerns, deeming provisions, at least the ones that that facilitate understanding about the law and its functions and impart justice are sometimes indispensable to legal thinking. With deemed approvals unequivocal responsibility could be affixed with the decision makers and relevant agencies, to allocate their resources appropriately and fulfill their roles within the expected time frames. The expectation is that, following this, social and economic benefits flow, with greater clarity and certainty for the applicants as well as speedier on-the ground provision. 60. In the case of R. vs Verrette, 2 SCR 838 (Supreme Court of Canada) at p. 845, Beetz, J. (1978), it was held that 'A deeming provision is a statutory fiction...A deeming provision artificially imports into a word or expression an additional meaning which they would not otherwise convey besides the normal meaning which they retain where they are used; it plays a function of enlargement analogous to the word "includes" in certain definitions...' 61. Clause 47(2) of the bye-law of the petitioner-Society provides to the effect: “সমবায় সমিতি আইনের/২০০১ ও সংশোধনী/২০০২ এবং বিধিমালার নিয়মানুযায়ী সাধারণ সভায় এই সকল উপ-আইনের কোন একটি বা একাধিক উপ-ধারা পরিবর্তন, নাকচ ও সংশোধন অথবা পুনঃপ্রণয়ন করা যাইবে । তবে এইরূপ পরিবর্তন, নাকচ, সংশোধন বা উপ-আইন পুনধপ্ণয়ন, নিবন্ধক কর্তৃক রেজিস্ট্রিকৃত না হওয়া পর্যন্ত কার্যকর বা বৈধ হইবে না।” 62. The nature and objects of the Bank and Co-operatives are not fully unison or similar. In this case, the petitioner by the stroke of a pen amended its bye-law and submitted it to Registrar on 30-4-2012 for approval and on 18-7-2012 by its Special General Meeting decided to open 75 branches throughout the country and started functioning. In view of clause 29Ga of the bye-law of the Society before convening Special General Meeting it is pre-condition to obtain a direction of the Registrar. Without any order of the Registrar, the aforesaid meeting was convened and the decision was taken to open branches and thereby, nakedly flouted the provisions of the bye-law of the petitioner-Society, though the petitioner is legally bound to follow its bye-law. 63. To sum up, our final conclusion is that- i. It appears that the Samabay Samity amendment Bill was introduced into the parliament by the Government on 11-9-2012 and the Bill was passed on 6-2-2013 and it came into force as law on 17-2-2013. Law making is a long process in our country. Before introducing the Bill, as per Rules of Business 1996 and Allocation of Business among the different Ministries and Divisions, the concerned Ministry has to make the initial draft and the same needs policy decisions of the Cabinet and thereafter, it has to send to the Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs for vetting. After vetting and before laying it to the parliament by the concerned Minister, it needs final approval of the Cabinet and, as such, it entails huge time at the concerned Ministry. The Registrar by his letter dated 15-3-2010 under Memo No. Ain-10/2009-74(Gov:) submitted draft proposal of the amendment of the Ain, 2001 to the Secretary, Rural Development and Co-operatives Division. In the aforesaid letter, the backdrop of amendment of the Ain, 2001 was clearly stated. It appears from the letter that the Parliamentary Standing Committee of the concerned Ministry by its meeting dated 29-7-2009 decided to amend the Ain, 2001 and the Bidhimala, 2004 to make them Samabay Bandhab. In this case, being aware of the process of the amendment of the Ain, 2001, Board of Directors of the petitioner-Society took decision very quickly on 14-4-2012 for amending its bye-law and it was approved on 29-4-2012 by its Special General Meeting. Thereafter, the petitioner-Society filed an application to the Registrar on 30-4-2012 for certificate of approval and registration. By its Special General Meeting decided to change its registered office from Narayanganj to Dhaka and for opening branches of the petitioner-Society throughout the country and, as such, it started functioning as many as 75 different places of the country and thereafter, on 29-7-2012 the petitioner filed Writ Petition No. 10101 of 2012 and obtained the Rule and the order of status quo. Thereafter, it started banking business throughout the country with full swing. It comes to our notice that due to opening of the branches throughout the country by different societies including the instant petitioner-Society using the word Bank after its name deceiving the people at large, specially the poor and indigent. Undoubtedly, it is a matter of great concerned. In the above backdrop, it is our considered view that the petitioner-Society has not come with clean hands to have remedy under Article 102 of the Constitution rather to perpetuate its malafide acts took resort of Article 102 of the Constitution. ii. The provisions of the Ain, 2013 are not contrary to the fundamental rights as enshrined in the Constitution and against the scheme of the Ain, 2001, rather it is essential to meet the challenges of rapidly changing phenomenon of the globe. iii. The petitioner-Society has got no right to use the word Bank without prior approval of Bangladesh Bank. iv. Deeming clause as mentioned under proviso appertaining to section 13(1) of the Ain, 2001 does not ipso facto approve the proposed bye-law for the reasons: (a) as it was not the intention of the legislature; (b) it is against the provision of rule 12(2) of the Bidhimala, 2004; (c) it is also against the provisions of clause 47(2) of the bye-law of the petitioner-Society; (d) the Special General Meeting as mentioned above had not been held with the approval of the Registrar in view of clause 29(Ga) of the bye-law; (e) the proviso to section 13 of the Ain, 2001 was not reasonable; (f) the petitioner-Society cannot flout its own bye-law or cannot go behind its bye-law. v. In our country, registered Societies are increasing like toadstool or mushroom, therefore, the sooner pull the reins, the best. vi. The office of the Registrar needs continuous close supervision and monitoring as to whether the Co-operatives registered by its office are performing their duty in accordance with the law or not. vii. It is expected that office of the Registrar should be very vigilant in disposing of the application/representation/ petition for approval of amendment of bye-law of the Co-operatives with utmost expedition and sincerity in order to avoid unnecessary litigations. 64. Having regard to the facts and circumstances of the entire case and the legal position critically involved therein, we are of the view that the Rules are devoid of any substance and therefore, the Rules shall fall through. 65. As a result, the Rules of Writ Petition No. 10101 of 2012, Writ Petition No. 2310 of 2019 and Writ Petition No. 9936 of 2019 are discharged, however, without passing any order as to costs. The order of status quo granted earlier by this Court in Writ Petition No. 10101 of 2012 thus stands vacated and recalled. Let a copy of the judgment be communicated to the Governor, Bangladesh Bank and Registrar, Department of Co-operatives at once. End.
